> **A note on evaluation.** The code in this vignette is shown for illustration
> and is **not executed** when the vignette is built, so no figures or printed
> output are embedded here. Every chunk runs as-is against the bundled
> `demo_eres` dataset; copy them into an interactive session to reproduce the
> diagnostics locally.

## 1  A diagnostic question, not an inferential one

A fitted Cox model is only as trustworthy as the picture it paints. After a
stepwise covariate search settles on body weight as a predictor of the
time-to-event endpoint, the natural next question is diagnostic rather than
inferential: does the model's predicted survival actually track what we observe
in the data, stratum by stratum? In this vignette we fit an exposure–safety Cox
model to the bundled `demo_eres` cohort, attach human-readable weight labels
through a variable specification, and overlay observed Kaplan–Meier curves
against model predictions across weight strata. The emphasis is on getting the
overlay *right* — ensuring each predicted curve lands on the stratum it belongs
to, even when weight bins carry back-transformed labels such as "≤ 62" and
"> 80", and even when we ask for many narrow bins.

## 2  Setup

```{r load}
library(erSCM)
data("demo_eres")

demo_eres <- demo_eres |>
  dplyr::mutate(SEX = as.factor(SEX))
```

We define variable metadata once. `plot_cox_terms()` uses these labels for the
axis titles and stratum captions, so the units the analyst sees on the plot are
the units they specified here.

```{r var-spec}
my_spec <- parse_var_spec(c(
  CMAXss = "Cmax,ss (ng/mL)",
  WT     = "Body Weight (kg)",
  AGE    = "Age (years)"
))
```

## 3  Fit the Cox SCM

```{r fit-cox}
surv_fit <- scm_coxph(
  eres_data          = demo_eres,
  exposure_vars      = "CMAXss",
  covariates         = c("WT", "AGE"),
  dv_col             = "sim_status",
  time_col           = "sim_time",
  significance_level = c(0.05, 0.01),
  var_spec           = my_spec,
  center             = TRUE
)
```

## 4  Observed vs. predicted survival by weight stratum

`plot_cox_terms()` bins a numeric covariate into `n_bins` strata and, for each
stratum, overlays the observed Kaplan–Meier step curve against the
model-predicted survival curve with a confidence ribbon.

```{r plot-cox-default}
plot_cox_terms(surv_fit, "WT")
```

Each predicted curve is matched to its stratum **by identity**, not by relying
on an incidental ordering of the panels. That distinction matters as soon as the
labels are back-transformed to the original weight scale: a facet captioned
"> 80" carries the prediction computed for patients above 80 kg, and the
adjacent "≤ 62" facet carries the prediction for the lightest group. The panels
are laid out in ascending numeric order rather than alphabetical string order,
so "9–10" never sorts before "80–90".

## 5  Asking for finer strata

The same identity-based matching holds as the stratification becomes finer. Here
we request twelve narrow weight bins:

```{r plot-cox-fine, fig.height = 7}
plot_cox_terms(surv_fit, "WT", n_bins = 12)
```

With many bins the labels span a wide numeric range, which is exactly the case
where a purely lexicographic panel order would misorder the facets. The plot
keeps the strata in numeric sequence and keeps each observed/predicted pair
together.

## 6  The underlying data frame

Set `plot = FALSE` to obtain the tidy data behind the figure — one row per
time point, stratum, and curve origin. This is convenient for custom layouts or
for tabulating landmark survival probabilities.

```{r plot-cox-data}
cox_curves <- plot_cox_terms(surv_fit, "WT", plot = FALSE)
head(cox_curves)
```

The returned frame carries a `strata` column whose labels match the facet
captions exactly, and an `origin` column distinguishing the observed
Kaplan–Meier curve from the model prediction — the same identity link that the
plotted version relies on.

## 7  A note on quiet internals

Building these overlays involves several grouped summaries and joins. Those
internal steps are deliberately silent: `plot_cox_terms()` does not emit
`dplyr` "joining by" messages or grouped-output notes, so the function is safe to
call inside reports and loops without polluting the console.
